claim: Pairing noisy auditory speech with a video of the talker dramatically improves perception.
source: Pairing noisy auditory speech with a video of the talker dramatically improves perception (Bernstein et al., 2004; Grant and Seitz, 2000; Munhall et al., 2004; Ross et al., 2007; Sumby and Pollack, 1954).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research studies.

claim: Visual speech can provide a perceptual benefit because any particular mouth movement made by the talker is compatible with only a few auditory phonemes.
source: Visual speech can provide a perceptual benefit because any particular mouth movement made by the talker is compatible with only a few auditory phonemes (Cappelletta and Harte, 2012; Jeffers and Barley, 1971; Neti et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on phoneme-viseme compatibility.

claim: Viewing a rounded open-mouth shape allows the observer to rule out ~80% of phonemes incompatible with this mouth shape.
source: For instance, viewing a rounded open-mouth shape allows the observer to rule out the ~80% of phonemes incompatible with this mouth shape (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A which illustrates compatible and incompatible phonemes.

claim: Bayesian inference provides a plausible algorithm for how the observer combines the visual mouth shape and auditory phoneme information.
source: Bayesian inference provides a plausible algorithm for how the observer combines the visual mouth shape and auditory phoneme information (Ma et al., 2009; Magnotti and Beauchamp, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior theoretical and modeling work.

claim: Most audiovisual words provide a visual head start.
source: Although there is a range in the relative onset of auditory and visual speech, most audiovisual words provide a visual head start.
evidence: Based on the natural variability in temporal relationships between auditory and visual speech.

claim: In the word 'drive', the visual onset of the open mouth preceded auditory vocalization by 400 ms.
source: For instance, in an audiovisual recording of the word 'drive' (Figure 1B) the visual onset of the open mouth required to enunciate the initial 'd' of the word preceded auditory vocalization by 400 ms
evidence: Supported by measurements from the stimulus shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the word 'known', auditory voice onset occurred 100 ms before visible changes in the talker's mouth.
source: For instance, in an audiovisual recording of the word 'known', auditory voice onset occurred 100 ms before visible changes in the talker's mouth (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by measurements from the stimulus shown in Figure 1C.

claim: If the visual head start contributes to the perceptual benefits of visual speech, these benefits should be greater for mouth-leading words than for voice-leading words.
source: If the visual head start contributes to the perceptual benefits of visual speech, these benefits should be greater for mouth-leading words than for voice-leading words.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis about the visual head start.

claim: Studies of patients with cortical lesions have implicated a network of brain areas in occipital, temporal, frontal, and parietal cortex in speech perception.
source: Studies of patients with cortical lesions (Hickok et al., 2018; Stasenko et al., 2015) and fMRI, MEG, EEG, and electrocorticographic (intracranial EEG) studies have implicated a network of brain areas in occipital, temporal, frontal, and parietal cortex (Crosse et al., 2016; Hickok and Poeppel, 2015; Okada et al., 2013; Salmelin, 2007; Shahin et al., 2018; Sohoglu and Davis, 2016; van Wassenhove et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior neuroimaging and lesion studies.

claim: Posterior superior temporal gyrus and sulcus (pSTG) are responsive to both unisensory auditory speech and unisensory visual speech.
source: Within this network, posterior superior temporal gyrus and sulcus (pSTG) are responsive to both unisensory auditory speech (Belin et al., 2000; Formisano et al., 2008; Mesgarani et al., 2014) and unisensory visual speech (Bernstein et al., 2011; Bernstein and Liebenthal, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: pSTG contains subregions responsive to both auditory and visual speech.
source: with subregions responsive to both auditory and visual speech (Beauchamp et al., 2004; Ozker et al., 2017; Ozker et al., 2018a; Rennig et al., 2018; Zhu and Beauchamp, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: For mouth-leading words, viewing the face of the talker increased the intelligibility of noisy auditory speech by 23%, from 3% for auditory-only words to 26% for audiovisual words.
source: For mouth-leading words, viewing the face of the talker increased the intelligibility of noisy auditory speech by 23%, from 3% for auditory-only words to 26% for audiovisual words (odds-ratio 0.00 for auditory vs. 0.07 for audiovisual; p<10−16).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the first perceptual experiment with statistical analysis.

claim: For voice-leading words, viewing the face of the talker provided only a 10% accuracy increase, from 14% to 24%.
source: For voice-leading words, viewing the face of the talker provided only a 10% accuracy increase, from 14% to 24% (odds-ratio 0.03 vs. 0.09, p=10−9).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the first perceptual experiment with statistical analysis.

claim: The interaction between format and word type was significant in the first perceptual experiment (p=10−14).
source: The interaction between format and word type was significant (p=10−14).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the first perceptual experiment, there were significant main effects of format (p<10−16) and word type (p=10−15) driven by higher accuracy for audiovisual words and for voice-leading words.
source: In addition to the interaction, there were significant main effects of format (p<10−16) and word type (p=10−15) driven by higher accuracy for audiovisual words and for voice-leading words.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the second perceptual experiment, for mouth-leading words, viewing the face of the talker increased the intelligibility of noisy auditory speech by 59%, from 6% for auditory-only words to 65% for audiovisual words.
source: For these mouth-leading words, viewing the face of the talker increased the intelligibility of noisy auditory speech by 59%, from 6% for auditory-only words to 65% for audiovisual words (odds-ratio 0.01 vs. 2.24, p<10−16).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the second perceptual experiment with statistical analysis.

claim: In the second perceptual experiment, for voice-leading words, viewing the face of the talker provided only a 37% accuracy increase, from 23% to 60%.
source: For voice-leading words, viewing the face of the talker provided only a 37% accuracy increase, from 23% to 60% (odds-ratio 0.17 vs. 1.66, p<10−16).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the second perceptual experiment with statistical analysis.

claim: The interaction between format and word type was significant in the second perceptual experiment (p<10−16).
source: The interaction between format and word type was significant (p<10−16) driven by the larger benefit of visual speech for mouth-leading words.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the second perceptual experiment, there was a significant main effect of format (p<10−16) and word type (p=0.04) driven by higher accuracy for audiovisual words and for voice-leading words.
source: In addition to the interaction, there was a significant main effect of format (p<10−16) and word type (p=0.04) driven by higher accuracy for audiovisual words and for voice-leading words.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Neural responses were recorded from 28 electrodes implanted over the posterior superior temporal gyrus (pSTG) of eight epileptic patients.
source: in eight epileptic participants we recorded from electrodes implanted bilaterally over the posterior superior temporal gyrus (pSTG) that showed a significant response to auditory-only speech measured as the percent increase in the power of the high-frequency (75 to 150 Hz) electrical activity relative to baseline (n = 28 electrodes, locations and auditory-only response magnitude shown in Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data collection and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The neural response to auditory-only speech was measured as the percent increase in the power of the high-frequency (75 to 150 Hz) electrical activity relative to baseline.
source: that showed a significant response to auditory-only speech measured as the percent increase in the power of the high-frequency (75 to 150 Hz) electrical activity relative to baseline
evidence: This describes the measurement method used in the neural experiments.

claim: The neural response to auditory-only and audiovisual speech in pSTG began shortly after auditory speech onset at 0 ms, peaked at 180 ms, and returned to baseline after auditory speech offset at 550 ms.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, the neural response to the single word stimuli in the pSTG began shortly after auditory speech onset at 0 ms, peaked at 180 ms, and returned to baseline after auditory speech offset at 550 ms.
evidence: Supported by neural data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The response to audiovisual mouth-leading words was 34% smaller than the response to auditory-only mouth-leading words (118% vs. 152%, p=10−5).
source: As shown in Figure 3C, the response to audiovisual mouth-leading words was 34% smaller than the response to auditory-only mouth-leading words (118% vs. 152%, p=10−5).
evidence: Supported by neural data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The response to audiovisual voice-leading words was not significantly different than the response to auditory-only voice-leading words (129% vs. 134%, p=0.4).
source: In contrast, the response to audiovisual voice-leading words was not significantly different than the response to auditory-only voice-leading words (129% vs. 134%, p=0.4).
evidence: Supported by neural data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The interaction between word format and word type was significant in the neural data (p=0.003).
source: This interaction between word format and word type was significant (p=0.003).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of neural data.

claim: There were significant main effects of word format (p=10−6) and word type (p=0.01) in the neural data, driven by larger responses for auditory-only words and for mouth-leading words.
source: There were also significant main effects of word format (p=10−6, driven by larger responses for auditory-only words) and word type (p=0.01, driven by larger responses for mouth-leading words).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of neural data.

claim: There was a significant positive response to visual-only words in pSTG, with a mean amplitude of 20% (0 to 200 ms after visual speech onset; p=10−7).
source: There was a significant positive response to visual-only words, with a mean amplitude of 20% (0 to 200 ms after visual speech onset; significantly greater than baseline, p=10−7, single sample t-test).
evidence: Supported by neural data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: 27 out of 28 electrodes showed a positive response to visual-only speech.
source: The effect was consistent across electrodes, with 27 out of 28 electrodes showing a positive response to visual-only speech, demonstrating that information about visual speech reaches pSTG.
evidence: Supported by neural data analysis across electrodes.

claim: The pSTG response to visual speech features occurred ~100 ms earlier than the response to auditory speech features.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, the pSTG response to visual speech features occurred ~100 ms earlier than the response to auditory speech features, sufficient time for substantial multisensory interactions to occur.
evidence: Supported by neural data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Responses to visual-only speech occurred a mean of 123 ms earlier than the response to auditory-only speech (p=10−8).
source: Responses were aligned to auditory onset (or to the time when auditory onset would have occurred for visual-only stimuli), with the response to visual-only speech occurring a mean of 123 ms earlier than the response to auditory-only speech (paired t-test, p=10−8).
evidence: Supported by neural data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: For 25 out of 28 electrodes, the response to visual-only mouth-leading words occurred earlier than the response to auditory-only mouth-leading words.
source: For 25 out of 28 electrodes, the response to visual-only mouth-leading words occurred earlier than the response to auditory-only mouth-leading words.
evidence: Supported by neural data analysis across electrodes.

claim: There was a significant positive relationship across electrodes between early visual response and multisensory influence for mouth-leading words (r = 0.64, p=10−4).
source: As shown in Figure 4B, there was a significant positive relationship across electrodes between early visual response and multisensory influence (r = 0.64, p=10−4).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of neural data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For voice-leading words, the latency of the visual-only and auditory-only neural responses were similar (mean latency 11 ms later for visual-only vs. auditory-only speech, p=0.77).
source: For voice-leading words, the latency of the visual-only and auditory-only neural responses were similar (mean latency 11 ms later for visual-only vs. auditory-only speech, p=0.77)
evidence: Supported by neural data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: For voice-leading words, there was not a significant correlation between visual-only response amplitude and multisensory influence across electrodes (r = 0.18, p=0.35).
source: across electrodes there was not a significant correlation between visual-only response amplitude and multisensory influence, defined as the difference between the audiovisual vs. auditory-only neural responses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; r = 0.18, p=0.35).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of neural data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Latencies were similar for auditory-only mouth-leading vs. voice-leading words (128 ms vs. 134 ms, p=0.54).
source: Latencies were similar for auditory-only mouth-leading vs. voice-leading words (128 ms vs. 134 ms, p=0.54) demonstrating that the alignment of responses to the physical onset of speech was effective.
evidence: Supported by neural data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: No consistent organization of multisensory influence was observed when electrodes were viewed on the cortical surface.
source: When viewed on the cortical surface, no consistent organization of multisensory influence was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by anatomical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The benefit of visual speech was significantly greater for mouth-leading words than for voice-leading words.
source: However, the benefit of visual speech was significantly greater for mouth-leading words, demonstrating that the visual head start enhances perception beyond the mere availability of visual information.
evidence: Inferred from the perceptual experiment results showing interaction effects.

claim: When visual speech was present for mouth-leading words, the neural response decreased.
source: Surprisingly, when visual speech was present for mouth-leading words, the neural response decreased, the opposite of the increased accuracy observed perceptually.
evidence: Supported by neural data showing reduced responses to audiovisual vs. auditory-only mouth-leading words.

claim: The pSTG contains populations selective for specific phonemes.
source: To better understand these results, we constructed a post hoc neural model that builds on the experimental observation that the pSTG contains populations selective for specific phonemes (Formisano et al., 2008; Hamilton et al., 2018; Mesgarani et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies showing phoneme selectivity in pSTG.

claim: For mouth-leading words, the early availability of visual information enhances responses in neurons representing phonemes that are compatible with the visual speech and suppresses neurons representing phonemes that are incompatible with the visual speech.
source: The key feature of the model is that for mouth-leading words (words with a visual head start) the early availability of visual information enhances responses in neurons representing phonemes that are compatible with the visual speech and suppresses neurons representing phonemes that are incompatible with the visual speech.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from the post hoc neural model.

claim: In all published classifications, there are more incompatible than compatible phonemes for any particular viseme.
source: In all published classifications, there are more incompatible than compatible phonemes for any particular viseme (Cappelletta and Harte, 2012; Jeffers and Barley, 1971; Neti et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior classification studies.

claim: The visual head start decreases the total response since more neuronal populations are suppressed than are enhanced.
source: Therefore, the visual head start decreases the total response since more neuronal populations are suppressed than are enhanced.
evidence: This is a prediction from the neural model based on the ratio of incompatible to compatible phonemes.

claim: For voice-leading speech, there is less time for the suppression and enhancement of incompatible and compatible phonemes to manifest, resulting in similar responses to audiovisual and auditory-only voice-leading words.
source: For voice-leading speech such as the audiovisual syllable 'm' (Figure 5D) there is less time for the suppression and enhancement of incompatible and compatible phonemes to manifest, resulting in similar responses to audiovisual and auditory-only voice-leading words.
evidence: This is an explanation from the neural model illustrated in Figure 5D.

claim: Only suppression was observed in 25/28 pSTG electrodes.
source: However, only suppression was observed in 25/28 pSTG electrodes (the remaining three electrodes showed similar responses to audiovisual and auditory-only speech).
evidence: Supported by neural data analysis across electrodes.

claim: The relatively large recording electrodes recorded the summed responses of a combination of many suppressed populations and a few enhanced populations.
source: If we assume that our relatively large recording electrodes recorded the summed responses of a combination of many suppressed populations and a few enhanced populations, the net effect should be suppression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neural data based on electrode properties.

claim: Silent viewing of the visual syllable 'ga' does not produce an auditory percept, but when paired with the auditory syllable 'ba', many participants report hearing 'da'.
source: For instance, silent viewing of the visual syllable 'ga' does not produce an auditory percept, but when paired with the auditory syllable 'ba', many participant report hearing 'da' (Mallick et al., 2015; McGurk and MacDonald, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on the McGurk effect.

claim: The pSTG response to visual-only speech is much weaker than the response to auditory speech.
source: Neurally, this could reflect the fact that although the pSTG responds to visual-only speech, the response is much weaker than the response to auditory speech (note the different scales for the different modalities in Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by neural data shown in Figure 4A with different scales for visual and auditory responses.

claim: The significant correlation between the amplitude of the visual response and the degree of multisensory modulation supports the case that there is an interaction between visual and auditory speech information in pSTG.
source: In either case, the significant correlation between the amplitude of the visual response and the degree of multisensory modulation bolsters the case that there is an interaction between visual and auditory speech information in pSTG.
evidence: Based on the correlation analysis reported earlier in the results.

claim: Audiovisual speech selectively enhances activity in regions of early visual cortex representing the mouth of the talker.
source: In an earlier study, we demonstrated that audiovisual speech selectively enhances activity in regions of early visual cortex representing the mouth of the talker (Ozker et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: Interactions between auditory and visual speech can occur both relatively early in processing ('early integration') and at both early and late stages ('multistage integration').
source: These findings support the idea that interactions between auditory and visual speech can occur both relatively early in processing ('early integration') and at both early and late stages ('multistage integration') as proposed by Peelle and Sommers (2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to a prior theoretical framework and the current findings.

claim: Information about visual mouth movements arrives in pSTG from more posterior regions of lateral temporal cortex.
source: Since cortex in superior temporal gyrus and sulcus receives inputs from earlier stages of the auditory and visual processing hierarchies, it seems probable that information about visual mouth movements arrives in pSTG from more posterior regions of lateral temporal cortex (Bernstein et al., 2008; Zhu and Beauchamp, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies and anatomical knowledge.

claim: Information about auditory phonemic content arrives in pSTG from posterior belt areas of auditory cortex.
source: while information about auditory phonemic content arrives in pSTG from posterior belt areas of auditory cortex (Leaver and Rauschecker, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to a prior study and anatomical knowledge.

claim: Cross-modal interactions are harnessed by all levels of the cortical processing hierarchy in the service of perception and cognition.
source: Together with previous work showing that visual cortex is modulated by auditory speech (Ozker et al., 2018b; Schepers et al., 2015), the present results from the pSTG provide another example of how cross-modal interactions are harnessed by all levels of the cortical processing hierarchy in the service of perception and cognition (Ghazanfar and Schroeder, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies and the current findings.

claim: Mechanical Turk and in-laboratory testing produce similar results for experiments examining multisensory speech perception.
source: Previously, we have shown that Mechanical Turk and in-laboratory testing produces similar results for experiments examining multisensory speech perception (Magnotti et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to a prior validation study.

claim: All experiments were approved by the Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects at Baylor College of Medicine.
source: All experiments were approved by the Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects at Baylor College of Medicine.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Eight subjects (5F, mean age 36, 6L hemisphere) who were selected to undergo intracranial electrode grid placement for phase two epilepsy monitoring provided informed consent to participate in this research protocol.
source: Eight subjects (5F, mean age 36, 6L hemisphere) who were selected to undergo intracranial electrode grid placement for phase two epilepsy monitoring provided informed consent to participate in this research protocol.
evidence: This describes the participant demographics and consent process.

claim: Implanted electrodes consisted of platinum alloy discs embedded in flexible silastic sheets.
source: Implanted electrodes consisted of platinum alloy discs embedded in flexible silastic sheets (Ad-Tech Corporation, Racine, WI).
evidence: This describes the electrode materials and manufacturer.

claim: Only electrodes with 2.3 mm diameter exposed surfaces were included in the analysis.
source: Electrodes with both 2.3 mm and 0.5 mm diameter exposed surfaces were implanted, but only electrodes with 2.3 mm were included in this analysis.
evidence: This describes an inclusion criterion for the analysis.

claim: A reversed intracranial electrode facing the skull was used as a reference for recording.
source: A reversed intracranial electrode facing the skull was used as a reference for recording
evidence: This describes the recording reference method.

claim: All signals were amplified, filtered (high-pass 0.3 Hz first-order Butterworth, low pass 500 Hz fourth-order Butterworth), digitized at 2000 Hz.
source: and all signals were amplified, filtered (high-pass 0.3 Hz first-order Butterworth, low pass 500 Hz fourth-order Butterworth), digitized at 2000 Hz
evidence: This describes the signal processing parameters.

claim: Preprocessing was performed using the R Analysis and Visualization of intracranial Electroencephalography (RAVE) package.
source: Preprocessing was performed using the R Analysis and Visualization of intracranial Electroencephalography (RAVE) package (https://openwetware.org/wiki/Beauchamp:RAVE).
evidence: This describes the software used for preprocessing.

claim: Data was notch filtered (60 Hz and harmonics), referenced to the average of all valid channels, and converted into frequency and phase domains using a wavelet transform.
source: Data was notch filtered (60 Hz and harmonics), referenced to the average of all valid channels, and converted into frequency and phase domains using a wavelet transform.
evidence: This describes the preprocessing steps.

claim: The number of cycles of the wavelet was increased as a function of frequency, from 3 cycles at 2 Hz to 20 cycles at 200 Hz, to optimize tradeoff between temporal and frequency precision.
source: The number of cycles of the wavelet was increased as a function of frequency, from 3 cycles at 2 Hz to 20 cycles at 200 Hz, to optimize tradeoff between temporal and frequency precision (Cohen, 2014).
evidence: This describes the wavelet parameters with citation to methodological reference.

claim: Data was down-sampled to 100 Hz after the wavelet transform.
source: Data was down-sampled to 100 Hz after the wavelet transform.
evidence: This describes a data processing step.

claim: The continuous data was epoched into trials using the auditory speech onset of each stimulus as the reference (t = 0).
source: The continuous data was epoched into trials using the auditory speech onset of each stimulus as the reference (t = 0).
evidence: This describes the epoching procedure.

claim: For visual-only trials, t = 0 was considered to be the same time at which the auditory speech would have begun, as determined from the corresponding audiovisual stimulus.
source: For visual-only trials, t = 0 was considered to be the same time at which the auditory speech would have begun, as determined from the corresponding audiovisual stimulus.
evidence: This describes the time alignment procedure for visual-only trials.

claim: For each trial and frequency, the power data were transformed into percentage signal change from baseline, where baseline was set to the average power of the response from −1.4 to −0.4 s prior to auditory speech onset.
source: For each trial and frequency, the power data were transformed into percentage signal change from baseline, where baseline was set to the average power of the response from −1.4 to −0.4 s prior to auditory speech onset.
evidence: This describes the baseline normalization procedure.

claim: The percent signal change from baseline was averaged over frequencies from 75 to 150 Hz to calculate the broadband high-frequency activity (BHA).
source: The percent signal change from this pre-stimulus baseline was then averaged over frequencies from 75 to 150 Hz to calculate the broadband high-frequency activity (BHA).
evidence: This describes the calculation of the BHA measure.

claim: Trials with median absolute differences more than five standard deviations from the mean were excluded (<2% excluded trials).
source: Trials with median absolute differences more than five standard deviations from the mean were excluded (<2% excluded trials).
evidence: This describes the outlier exclusion criterion.

claim: FreeSurfer was used to construct cortical surface models for each subject from their preoperative structural T1 magnetic resonance image scans.
source: FreeSurfer (Dale et al., 1999; Fischl et al., 1999) was used to construct cortical surface models for each subject from their preoperative structural T1 magnetic resonance image scans.
evidence: This describes the anatomical reconstruction method with citations.

claim: Post-implantation CT brain scans were aligned to the preoperative structural MRI brain using the Analysis of Functional Neuroimaging (AFNI) package.
source: Post-implantation CT brain scans, showing the location of the intracranial electrodes, were then aligned to the preoperative structural MRI brain using the Analysis of Functional Neuroimaging (AFNI; Cox, 1996) package
evidence: This describes the image alignment method with citation.

claim: Electrode positions were marked manually on the structural surface model.
source: and electrode positions were marked manually on the structural surface model.
evidence: This describes the electrode localization procedure.

claim: Electrode locations were projected to the surface of the cortical model using AFNI.
source: Electrode locations were projected to the surface of the cortical model using AFNI.
evidence: This describes the projection method.

claim: SUMA was used to visualize cortical surface models with overlaid electrodes.
source: SUMA (Argall et al., 2006) was used to visualize cortical surface models with overlaid electrodes
evidence: This describes the visualization method with citation.

claim: Positions were confirmed using intraoperative photographs of the electrode grids overlaid on the brain when available.
source: and positions were confirmed using intraoperative photographs of the electrode grids overlaid on the brain when available.
evidence: This describes the validation method for electrode localization.

claim: Cortical surface models with overlaid electrodes were mapped to the Colin N27 brain using AFNI/SUMA.
source: Cortical surface models with overlaid electrodes were mapped to the Colin N27 brain (Holmes et al., 1998) using AFNI/SUMA, allowing for visualization of electrodes from all subjects overlaid over one single brain atlas.
evidence: This describes the normalization to a standard brain with citation.

claim: All analyses were performed on electrodes that met both an anatomical criterion (located over the posterior superior temporal gyrus) and a functional criterion (significant BHA response to auditory-only speech).
source: All analyses were performed on electrodes (n = 28 from eight participants; Figure 3A) that met both an anatomical criterion (located over the posterior superior temporal gyrus) and a functional criterion (significant BHA response to auditory-only speech).
evidence: This describes the electrode selection criteria.

claim: The anatomical border between anterior and posterior superior temporal gyrus was defined by extending a line inferiorly from the central sulcus to split the superior temporal gyrus into anterior and posterior portions.
source: The anatomical border between anterior and posterior superior temporal gyrus was defined by extending a line inferiorly from the central sulcus to split the superior temporal gyrus into anterior and posterior portions.
evidence: This describes the anatomical definition used.

claim: The functional criterion was a significant (p<0.001, Bonferroni-corrected) BHA response to the auditory-only word format during the period from stimulus onset to stimulus offset (0 s to 0.55 s).
source: The functional criterion was a significant (p<0.001, Bonferroni-corrected) BHA response to the auditory-only word format during the period from stimulus onset to stimulus offset (0 s to 0.55 s).
evidence: This describes the functional selection criterion.

claim: The main comparison of interest (the interaction between response amplitude for different word types and stimulus word formats) was independent of the functional criterion and hence unbiased.
source: Because the functional criterion ignored word type (voice-leading vs. mouth-leading) and did not include audiovisual stimuli, the main comparison of interest (the interaction between response amplitude for different word types and stimulus word formats) was independent of the functional criterion and hence unbiased.
evidence: This explains why the selection criterion does not bias the main analysis.

claim: Neural responses were collapsed into a single value by averaging the high-frequency activity (BHA) across the time window from stimulus onset to stimulus offset (0 s to 0.55 s) for each trial for each electrode.
source: Neural responses were collapsed into a single value by averaging the high-frequency activity (BHA) across the time window from stimulus onset to stimulus offset (0 s to 0.55 s) for each trial for each electrode.
evidence: This describes the data reduction procedure for statistical analysis.

claim: A linear mixed-effects model (LME) was used to analyze neural responses with fixed effects of word format and word type, their interaction, and random effects of electrode nested within subject.
source: These values were then analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model (LME) with a baseline of mouth-leading words in the auditory-only word format. The model factors were two fixed effects of word format (auditory-only vs. audiovisual) and word type (mouth-leading vs. voice-leading), a word format-by-word type interaction was included, as well as random effects of electrode nested within subject (random intercepts and slopes for each subject-by-electrode pair).
evidence: This describes the statistical model used for neural data analysis.

claim: All LMEs were performed in R using the lmer function in the lme4 package.
source: All LMEs were performed in R using the lmer function in the lme4 package.
evidence: This describes the software used for statistical analysis.

claim: Estimated p-values were calculated using the Satterthwaite approximation provided by the lmerTest package.
source: Estimated p-values were calculated using the Satterthwaite approximation provided by the lmerTest package (Kuznetsova et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the method for calculating p-values with citation.

claim: The visual head start enhances perception beyond the mere availability of visual information.
source: However, the benefit of visual speech was significantly greater for mouth-leading words, demonstrating that the visual head start enhances perception beyond the mere availability of visual information.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the perceptual experiment results.

claim: The presence of visual speech suppressed responses to auditory speech, more so for words with a visual head start.
source: The presence of visual speech suppressed responses to auditory speech, more so for words with a visual head start.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the neural results.

claim: The head start inhibits representations of incompatible auditory phonemes, increasing perceptual accuracy and decreasing total neural responses.
source: We suggest that the head start inhibits representations of incompatible auditory phonemes, increasing perceptual accuracy and decreasing total neural responses.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism stated in the abstract.

claim: Multisensory interactions are a powerful modulator of activity throughout the speech perception network.
source: Together with previous work showing visual cortex modulation (Ozker et al., 2018b) these results from pSTG demonstrate that multisensory interactions are a powerful modulator of activity throughout the speech perception network.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on current and prior findings.

claim: Humans must understand speech both quickly (at rates of ~5 syllables a second) and accurately.
source: This extra processing time is important because humans must understand speech both quickly (as speech is generated rapidly, at rates of ~5 syllables a second) and accurately (as errors in communication are potentially costly).
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about speech processing demands.

claim: A second potential reason for the perceptual benefit of visual speech is that visual speech can provide a head start on perception when mouth movements begin before auditory vocalization.
